sections.h2: Where does Jefferson County sit on the Florida map?
sections.html:
Jefferson County is a rural Big Bend county that the county website calls the Keystone County, because it is the only Florida county reaching from the Georgia line to the Gulf coast. It was established in 1827, and about 14,000 people live in roughly 609 square miles of farms, ranches and timberland.

Monticello, the county seat, sits 25 miles east of Tallahassee. Three rivers cross the county: the Wacissa, the Aucilla and the St. Marks. Lake Miccosukee covers 6,200 acres in the northwest corner, and the St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge holds nearly 9,000 acres near the coast. Interstate 10 and five U.S. highways cross it, and commercial flights leave from Tallahassee, 35 miles away.

For an owner, the layout matters for taxes. A town lot in Monticello, a farm parcel in the north and a coastal tract do not sit in the same taxing districts, so two Jefferson County bills rarely look alike.

sections.h2: Who sends and who reads a Jefferson County tax bill?
sections.html:
Three independent offices share the work, and the county's own page points to jeffersonpa.net for parcel search and exemption filing.

  • Property Appraiser: sets the assessed value and takes exemption applications.
  • Tax Collector: mails statements on or before November 1, accepts payment and runs the certificate sale.
  • Clerk and Comptroller: keeps official records and conducts a tax deed auction if one is requested.

Each August the appraiser mails a TRIM notice with the parcel's value and the rates each taxing body proposes. The hearings printed on it happen before rates are set in September.

sections.h2: Which millage lines did the collector list for 2026?
sections.html:
The Tax Collector's millage page shows six lines. A house inside Monticello would see all six, while a rural parcel skips the city line. The collector's glossary defines one mill as one-tenth of a cent, or a dollar per thousand of taxable value.

sections.h2: What does the Jefferson County calendar look like from November to June?
sections.html:
The mailing deadline is November 1, and the early payer gets 4 percent off in November, 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February. After that the clock runs toward April.

  • April 1: unpaid real estate tax is delinquent and takes a 3 percent penalty.
  • Early May: unpaid accounts are advertised in the local paper.
  • By June 1: the online certificate sale.

Tangible personal property, such as business equipment, draws a 1.5 percent monthly penalty once late. The collector's glossary adds that a year's lien attaches at the start of that year.

sections.h2: How do Jefferson County homestead and other exemptions work?
sections.html:
Homestead can cut $50,000 from the taxable figure, the first $25,000 reaching every levy and the second $25,000 sparing school levies. Form DR-501 goes to the appraiser before the March 1 cutoff, for a house that was your permanent home on January 1. Renting the house or moving out ends it.

An income-tested senior add-on, worth as much as $50,000, exists only where the local government chose to adopt it. Disabled veterans and deployed servicemembers have state-listed benefits as well. Ask the Jefferson County Property Appraiser which local options are in force. Annual growth in a homestead's assessed value is capped, and that cushion ends at a sale.

sections.h2: Does Jefferson County land use affect a sale?
sections.html:
It can. The county says building in Jefferson County is a two-step process: a Development Permit from the Planning Department first, then building permits from the Building Department, and no building permit issues for a site without the first. Land Development Regulations reach every kind of development, including driveways and power poles.

The page also warns that any subdivision of land needs approval under the Land Development Code, and that approval should be confirmed before new deeds are recorded. If land is conveyed without it, later owners may be unable to get a building permit. A seller splitting off acreage should check this before a buyer's attorney does.

  • The Planning Commission meets the second Thursday of each month at 6:00 p.m. in the Courthouse Annex, 435 West Walnut Street.
  • The county holds a Community Rating System score of 8 under the federal flood insurance program, which earns premium discounts.
  • The adopted Comprehensive Plan 2045 and its maps are posted on the county's planning page.

sections.h2: What shape does the land and climate give a Jefferson County parcel?
sections.html:
The county describes four seasons, a mean annual temperature of 67 degrees, January averages near 51 and July near 81, with rainfall near 57 inches annually. Red clay hills, live oaks and pasture define much of the open land, and the Monticello historic district holds 42 nineteenth-century buildings across 27 blocks. The 1890 Perkins Opera House and the 1910 courthouse anchor it.

Older and historic structures bring their own questions at sale time, such as roof age, wiring and flood zone. FEMA's Flood Map Service Center, which the county links, shows the zone for a given parcel.

sections.h2: How should a Jefferson County seller handle the tax balance?
sections.html:
The seller carries the tax to the closing date, and older unpaid years have to be cleared for clean title. The closing agent normally requests a payoff from the collector and pays it at the table from the seller's side.

The collector notes that the roll is a working roll and amounts can change during the year, so a quote is a snapshot. Get the payoff in writing with a date near closing. With an escrowing lender, ask how soon any leftover balance returns.

  • Search the parcel on the collector's site and note every year with a balance.
  • Ask whether a certificate was sold, since redemption takes certified funds.
  • Confirm exemptions with the appraiser so the title company prorates correctly.
  • The clerk records the deed and takes the stamp tax at the counter.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Jefferson County tax?
sections.html:
The debt is sold to an investor as a certificate, which the collector describes as a lien created by paying the delinquent tax, not a purchase of the property. The sale is a reverse auction on interest that starts at 18 percent and goes to the lowest bidder.

Certificates last seven years, and the face amount includes the 3 percent penalty, a 5 percent collector's commission and advertising costs. A homestead whose face value is under $250 is issued to the county at 18 percent instead of being sold. If the 22 month period passes, the parcel can go to a tax deed sale, which the clerk runs after the holder applies once two years have passed. The opening bid on a homestead includes half the latest assessed value. A March 31 deferral application date may help an owner at risk.

faqs.q: How big is Jefferson County, and where is the county seat?
faqs.a: About 609 square miles, with Monticello as the seat, 25 miles east of Tallahassee. The county says roughly 14,000 people live there.

faqs.q: When does unpaid Jefferson County real estate tax turn delinquent?
faqs.a: April 1 is the line, and a 3 percent penalty lands then. The local paper runs unpaid accounts in early May, and the online certificate sale follows by June 1.

faqs.q: Is the Monticello millage line on every Jefferson County bill?
faqs.a: No. The collector's 2026 list shows a separate Monticello line of .00685010, which applies to parcels inside the city only.

faqs.q: Can I build on Jefferson County land without a permit?
faqs.a: Yes. The county requires a Development Permit from Planning first, then building permits, and subdivisions need approval before new deeds are recorded.

faqs.q: Where do I file for homestead in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: At the appraiser's office or on jeffersonpa.net, on Form DR-501, before March 1. The county's property page points residents to jeffersonpa.net.
